Answer Questions Q1.07.4 and Q1.07.5 using the following data. Cayley-Hamilton Theorem states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Consider a matrix: \[A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

A set three linear equations with unknowns \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\) is shown below. \[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 21.432 & 34.432 \\ 17.587 & -1.348 & -1.865 \\ 0 & -2.663 & -1.803 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 56.042 \\ 02.631 \\ 05.952 \end{bmatrix}\] Decompose the coefficient matrix into an upper triangular matrix and then solve for the unknowns, \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\).
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Given the system of three linear equations in matrix form \(AX = B\): \[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 21.432 & 34.432 \\ 17.587 & -1.348 & -1.865 \\ 0 & -2.663 & -1.803 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 56.042 \\ 2.631 \\ 5.952 \end{bmatrix}\] We construct the initial augmented matrix block: \[\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 0 & 21.432 & 34.432 & 56.042 \\ 17.587 & -1.348 & -1.865 & 2.631 \\ 0 & -2.663 & -1.803 & 5.952 \end{array} \right]\] Step 1: Row Interchanging \[R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2\] \[\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 17.587 & -1.348 & -1.865 & 2.631 \\ 0 & 21.432 & 34.432 & 56.042 \\ 0 & -2.663 & -1.803 & 5.952 \end{array} \right]\] Step 2: Upper Triangular Reduction \[R_3 \to R_3 - \left(\frac{-2.663}{21.432}\right)R_2 \implies R_3 \to R_3 + 0.124253 \cdot R_2\] Let us compute the updated entries for the third row up to three decimal places:
  • Entry \((3,2)\): \(-2.663 + (0.124253)(21.432) = 0\)
  • Entry \((3,3)\): \(-1.803 + (0.124253)(34.432) = -1.803 + 4.278 = 2.475\)
  • Augmented constant entry: \(5.952 + (0.124253)(56.042) = 5.952 + 6.963 = 12.915\)
This yields the finalized upper triangular augmented matrix configuration: \[\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} 17.587 & -1.348 & -1.865 & 2.631 \\ 0 & 21.432 & 34.432 & 56.042 \\ 0 & 0 & 2.475 & 12.915 \end{array} \right]\] Step 3: Back-Substitution 1. From the updated third row equation: \[2.475 \cdot Z = 12.915 \implies Z = \frac{12.915}{2.475} \approx 5.218\] 2. From the updated second row equation, substitute \(Z = 5.218\): \[21.432 \cdot Y + 34.432 \cdot Z = 56.042\] \[21.432 \cdot Y + 34.432(5.218) = 56.042\] \[21.432 \cdot Y + 179.667 = 56.042\] \[21.432 \cdot Y = 56.042 - 179.667 = -123.625\] \[Y = \frac{-123.625}{21.432} \approx -5.768\] 3. From the first row equation, substitute \(Y = -5.768\) and \(Z = 5.218\): \[17.587 \cdot X - 1.348 \cdot Y - 1.865 \cdot Z = 2.631\] \[17.587 \cdot X - 1.348(-5.768) - 1.865(5.218) = 2.631\] \[17.587 \cdot X + 7.775 - 9.732 = 2.631\] \[17.587 \cdot X - 1.957 = 2.631\] \[17.587 \cdot X = 2.631 + 1.957 = 4.588\] \[X = \frac{4.588}{17.587} \approx 0.261\] \[\boxed{X = 0.261, \;\; Y = -5.768, \;\; Z = 5.218}\]

questions.question: For the circuit shown in figure, find the current through the resistance R connected between points a and b by Thevenin's theorem.
questions.explanation:
To find the current through the \(10\Omega\) resistor connected between terminals \(a\) and \(b\), first determine the Thevenin equivalent seen from terminals \(a\) and \(b\). Step 1: Find \(R_{th}\)
Deactivate all independent voltage sources by replacing them with short circuits. The \(15\Omega\) and \(5\Omega\) resistors are in parallel: \[15\parallel 5 = \frac{15\times5}{15+5} = 3.75\Omega\] This \(3.75\Omega\) is in series with the remaining \(5\Omega\): \[R = 3.75+5 = 8.75\Omega\] Hence, \[R_{th} = 10\parallel 8.75 = \frac{10\times8.75}{10+8.75} = 4.67\Omega\] Step 2: Find \(V_{th}\)
Open-circuit the \(10\Omega\) resistor between terminals \(a\) and \(b\). Let clockwise mesh currents in the upper and lower loops be \(I_1\) and \(I_2\), respectively. Applying KVL in the upper loop, \[-45+120+15I_1+(10+5)(I_1-I_2)=0\] \[30I_1-15I_2=-75 \tag{1}\] Applying KVL in the lower loop, \[(10+5)(I_2-I_1)+5I_2-20=0\] \[-15I_1+20I_2=20 \tag{2}\] Solving (1) and (2), \[I_1=-3.2\text{ A}, \qquad I_2=-1.4\text{ A}\] Now applying KVL between terminals \(a\) and \(b\), \[-45+V_{th}+10(I_1-I_2)=0\] \[V_{th}=63\text{ V}\] Step 3: Connect the load
The Thevenin equivalent is a \(63\text{ V}\) source in series with \(R_{th}=4.67\Omega\), supplying the load \(R=10\Omega\). \[I = \frac{V_{th}}{R_{th}+R} = \frac{63}{4.67+10}= 4.29\text{ A}\] \[\boxed{I=4.29\text{ A}}\]

questions.question: In the network system shown in figure, find the current through \(Z_3\) using nodal method. The values of voltages are given in volts and the impedances are given in ohms.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation: Let the voltage across the impedance \(Z_{3}\) be \(V\). Taking the common node of the two sources as the reference ground, the current \(I\) flowing through \(Z_{3}\) can be expressed as: \[I = \frac{V}{Z_{3}} = \frac{V}{j10}\] Writing Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at the essential node whose voltage is \(V\): \[\frac{V - 100 \angle 0^{\circ}}{6 + j8} + \frac{V}{j10} + \frac{V - 100 \angle -60^{\circ}}{6 - j8} = 0\] Grouping the coefficients of the node voltage variable \(V\): \[V \left( \frac{1}{6 + j8} + \frac{1}{j10} + \frac{1}{6 - j8} \right) = \frac{100 \angle 0^{\circ}}{6 + j8} + \frac{100 \angle -60^{\circ}}{6 - j8}\] Simplifying the admittances inside the parenthesis by rationalizing or using common denominators: \[V \left( \frac{6 - j8}{100} - \frac{j10}{100} + \frac{6 + j8}{100} \right) = 18.39 \angle -30^{\circ}\] \[V \left( \frac{12 - j10}{100} \right) = 18.39 \angle -30^{\circ}\] Solving for the complex node voltage value \(V\): \[V = 117.74 \angle 9.805^{\circ}\,\text{V}\] Now, calculating the branch current \(I\) passing through the inductive element branch: \[I = \frac{V}{j10} = \frac{117.74 \angle 9.805^{\circ}}{10 \angle 90^{\circ}}\] \[I = 11.77 \angle -80.19^{\circ}\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{11.77 \angle -80.19^{\circ}\,\text{A}}\]

questions.question: In the circuit shown in figure, ammeter \(A_2\) reads 12 A and \(A_3\) reads 9 A. \(A_1\) will read A.
questions.explanation: Considering ideal ammeters where the ammeter resistance is \(0\,\Omega\) (i.e., there is no voltage drop across them), the network reduces to a parallel combination of an inductor and a resistor. Because the branches are connected in parallel, the same reference voltage appears across both elements. The current through the resistive branch, \(I_{A2}\), remains perfectly in phase with the voltage, while the current through the inductive branch, \(I_{A3}\), lags behind the voltage by \(90^{\circ}\). Therefore, the two branch currents \(I_{A2}\) and \(I_{A3}\) are in quadrature phase relationship. Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) in phasor form: \[\vec{I}_{A1} = \vec{I}_{A2} + \vec{I}_{A3}\] Since the two current vectors are perpendicular to each other (\(90^{\circ}\) out of phase), the magnitude of the total entering current \(|I_{A1}|\) is calculated using the orthogonal vector addition formula: \[|I_{A1}| = \sqrt{|I_{A2}|^{2} + |I_{A3}|^{2}}\] Substituting the given values (\(I_{A2} = 9\,\text{A}\) and \(I_{A3} = 12\,\text{A}\)) into the equation: \[|I_{A1}| = \sqrt{9^{2} + 12^{2}}\] \[|I_{A1}| = \sqrt{81 + 144} = \sqrt{225} = 15\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{15}\]

questions.question: A series R-L-C circuit has the following parameter values. \(R=10\,\Omega\), L=0.01 H, C= 100 mF. The Q factor of the circuit at resonance is
questions.explanation: At electrical resonance, the resonant angular frequency \(\omega_0\) is defined as: \[\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\] The Quality factor (\(Q\)-factor) for a series RLC network is expressed as: \[Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R}\] Substituting the expression for \(\omega_0\) into the \(Q\)-factor equation: \[Q = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \cdot \frac{L}{R}\] \[Q = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}\] Substituting the given component parameters (\(R = 10\,\Omega\), \(L = 0.01\,\text{H}\), and \(C = 100 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{F}\)): \[Q = \frac{1}{10}\sqrt{\frac{0.01}{100 \times 10^{-3}}} = 0.03162\] \[\boxed{0.03162}\]

questions.question: The common mode voltage of a unity gain (voltage follower) op-amp buffer in terms of its output voltage \(V_0\) is
questions.explanation:
Common Mode Voltage Formula:
The common-mode input voltage is the average of the two input terminal voltages: \[V_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{2}(V_+ + V_-) = \frac{1}{2}(V_i + V_0)\] Voltage Follower Relation:
For an ideal voltage follower buffer circuit: \[V_i = V_0\] Substituting \(V_i = V_0\) into the expression: \[V_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{2}(V_0 + V_0) = V_0\] \[\boxed{V_0}\]

questions.question: For the circuit shown in figure, determine \(\dfrac{V_0(s)}{V_i(s)}\) and hence write the equations for the magnitude and phase response of \(\dfrac{V_0}{V_i}\). If the value of \(R_1\) is \(100\,\text{k}\Omega\) and of \(R\) is \(10\,\text{k}\Omega\), determine the value of \(C\) to obtain a phase shift to \(270^\circ\) between \(V_0\) and \(V_i\) for an input frequency of \(1000\,\text{rad/s}\).
questions.explanation:
Transfer Function Derivation:
Using superposition theorem: \[V_{o1} = V_i \left(-\frac{R_1}{R_1}\right) = -V_i\] Non-inverting terminal voltage \(V_+\) by voltage divider: \[V_+ = V_i \left(\frac{1/j\omega C}{R + 1/j\omega C}\right) = V_i \left(\frac{1}{1 + j\omega RC}\right)\] Output due to non-inverting terminal: \[V_{o2} = V_+ \left(1 + \frac{R_1}{R_1}\right) = 2V_i \left(\frac{1}{1 + j\omega RC}\right)\] Net output voltage \(V_0\): \[V_0 = V_{o1} + V_{o2} = V_i \left(\frac{1 - j\omega RC}{1 + j\omega RC}\right)\] \[\frac{V_0(s)}{V_i(s)} = \frac{1 - sRC}{1 + sRC}\] Phase Shift & Calculation of \(C\):
Magnitude and Phase Response: \[\left|\frac{V_0}{V_i}\right| = 1, \quad \phi = -2\tan^{-1}(\omega RC)\] Given \(\phi = 270^\circ \equiv -90^\circ\): \[-2\tan^{-1}(\omega RC) = -90^\circ \implies \tan^{-1}(\omega RC) = 45^\circ\] \[\omega RC = 1 \implies C = \frac{1}{\omega R}\] Given \(\omega = 1000\,\text{rad/s}\) and \(R = 10\,\text{k}\Omega = 10^4\,\Omega\): \[C = \frac{1}{1000 \times 10^4} = 10^{-7}\,\text{F} = 0.1\,\mu\text{F}\] \[\boxed{0.1\,\mu\text{F}}\]
Key points
  • All-Pass Filter: The given circuit acts as a first-order active phase shifter (all-pass filter) with a constant unity gain magnitude.
  • Phase Angle Formula: \(\phi = -2\tan^{-1}(\omega RC)\).

questions.question: For the circuit shown in figure, determine the input impedance \(Z\). assume the op-amp to be an ideal one.
questions.explanation:
Test Source Analysis:
To find the input impedance \(Z_i\), apply a test voltage source \(V_t\) at the input terminal and let \(I_t\) be the drawn test current. At the non-inverting terminal: \[V_+ = V_t\] Since no current enters the ideal op-amp input terminals, no current flows through the \(R-L\) branch. Thus: \[V_- = V_0\] By virtual short concept: \[V_- = V_+ \implies V_0 = V_t\] Input Impedance Calculation:
Applying KCL at the non-inverting terminal node: \[\frac{V_t - 0}{R_1} - I_t + \frac{V_t - V_0}{R_1} = 0\] Since \(V_0 = V_t\), the term \(\frac{V_t - V_0}{R_1} = 0\): \[\frac{V_t}{R_1} - I_t = 0 \implies \frac{V_t}{I_t} = R_1\] Therefore, the input impedance \(Z_i\) is: \[Z_i = \frac{V_t}{I_t} = R_1\] \[\boxed{R_1}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: For a \(J\)-\(K\) flip-flop, its \(J\) input is tied to its own \(\bar{Q}\) output and its \(K\) input is connected to its own \(Q\) output. If the flip-flop is fed with a clock of frequency 1,MHz, its \(Q\) output frequency will be MHz.
questions.explanation:
Given : Clock frequency, \(f_{\text{CLK}} = 1\text{ MHz}\) From figure, \(J_n = \bar{Q}_n\), \(K_n = Q_n\) For a \(J\)-\(K\) FF, the characteristic equation is given by, \[Q_{n+1} = J_n\bar{Q}_n + \bar{K}_n Q_n\] \[Q_{n+1} = \bar{Q}_n\bar{Q}_n + \bar{Q}_n Q_n = \bar{Q}_n + 0 = \bar{Q}_n\] The above given flip-flop counts only two states i.e. 0 and 1, hence it is MOD-2 counter. For any MOD-\(M\) counter, output frequency is given by, \[f_0 = \frac{f_{\text{CLK}}}{M} = \frac{10^6}{2}\text{ Hz} = 0.5\text{ MHz}\] Hence, the output frequency of \(Q\) will be 0.5 MHz.
Key points
  • With \(J = \bar{Q}\) and \(K = Q\): \(Q_{n+1} = \bar{Q}_n\) always (toggles on every clock pulse).
  • This configuration acts as a divide-by-2 circuit (MOD-2 counter), which halves the input clock frequency.

questions.question: The closed loop transfer function of a control system is given by \[\frac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{2(s - 1)}{(s + 2)(s + 1)}\] for a unit step input the output is
questions.explanation: For a unit step input, \(R(s) = \frac{1}{s}\). Therefore, the output response in the \(s\)-domain is: \[C(s) = \frac{2(s - 1)}{s(s + 2)(s + 1)}\] Using partial fraction expansion: \[C(s) = \frac{A}{s} + \frac{B}{s + 2} + \frac{C}{s + 1} =\frac{-1}{s} + \frac{-3}{s + 2} + \frac{4}{s + 1}\] Taking the inverse Laplace transform to obtain the time-domain output \(c(t)\): \[c(t) = -3e^{-2t} + 4e^{-t} - 1\] \[\boxed{(A) \ \ -3e^{-2t} + 4e^{-t} - 1}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: Match the following root locations of the characteristic Equations of second order systems with their corresponding Unit step responses of second order systems.
questions.note: Answer: A-T, B-S, C-P, D-R, E-Q
questions.explanation:
• A \(\to\) T: Real, distinct poles on the negative real half of the \(s\)-plane indicate an critically/overdamped stable system whose step response smoothly approaches a steady-state value without any oscillations.
  • B \(\to\) S: Complex conjugate poles in the left-half of the \(s\)-plane characterize an underdamped stable system, where the response exhibits decaying (damped) oscillations towards \(1.0\).
  • C \(\to\) P: Purely imaginary poles (on the \(j\omega\)-axis) correspond to an undamped system yielding sustained, fixed-amplitude periodic oscillations.
  • D \(\to\) R: Complex conjugate poles located in the right-half of the \(s\)-plane cause an underdamped unstable response characterized by exponentially growing oscillations.
  • E \(\to\) Q: Real poles situated on the positive real axis mean the system is completely unstable, and its output increases exponentially toward infinity without oscillating.
\[\boxed{\text{A-T, B-S, C-P, D-R, E-Q}}\]
Key points
  • Poles in the left-half \(s\)-plane produce bounded, stable transient behaviors.
  • Poles on the imaginary axis correspond to marginally stable boundaries with undamped periodic outputs.
  • Poles in the right-half \(s\)-plane lead to unbounded, unstable growing response characteristics.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: Closed loop stability implies that \([1 + G(s)H(s)]\) has only in the left half of the s-plane.
questions.note: Answer: zeros
questions.explanation:
The characteristic equation of a closed-loop system is : \(1 + G(s)H(s) = 0\) The closed-loop transfer function is expressed as: \(T(s) = \dfrac{G(s)}{1 + G(s)H(s)}\)
  • The roots of the denominator of \(T(s)\) determine the closed-loop poles, which are identical to the roots of the equation \(1 + G(s)H(s) = 0\). Correspondingly, these poles are the zeros of the function \(1 + G(s)H(s)\).
  • For a closed-loop system to be stable, all of its closed-loop poles (and thus the zeros of \(1 + G(s)H(s)\)) must lie strictly in the left half of the \(s\)-plane.
\[\boxed{\text{zeros}}\]

Common data for Q4.95.2, Q4.95.3, Q4.95.4 The characteristic equation for a certain feedback control system is given by \(s^4 + 20s^3 + 15s^2 + 2s + K = 0\)

What is the frequency in rad/sec at which the system will oscillate?
questions.note: Answer: 0.316 rad/sec
questions.explanation: The system will sustain continuous oscillations at the marginal stability limit, which occurs when the row of \(s^1\) becomes zero: \[29.8 - 20K = 0 \implies K_{\text{mar}} = 1.49\] Forming the auxiliary equation \(A(s) = 0\) from the row just above it (\(s^2\) row): \[14.9s^2 + K_{\text{mar}} = 0 \implies s^2 = -\frac{1.49}{14.9} = -0.1\] \[s = \pm j\sqrt{0.1} \approx \pm j0.316\,\text{rad/sec}\] \[\boxed{\omega = 0.316\,\text{rad/sec}}\]

There are exactly \(2\) sign changes. Hence 2 rrots lie in right half of the s-plane. \[\boxed{2}\]

questions.question: A spherical conductor of radius `\(a\)' with charge `\(q\)' is placed concentrically inside an uncharged and unearthed spherical conducting shell of inner and outer radii \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) respectively. Taking potential to be zero at infinity, the potential at any point \(P\) within the shell \((r_1<r<r_2)\) will be [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
The conducting shell is a perfect conductor. Hence, the electric field inside the conducting material is zero. \[\vec{E}=0\] Since \[\vec{E}=-\nabla V,\] zero electric field means that the electric potential remains constant everywhere inside the conducting shell. Hence, the potential of the inner surface is equal to the potential at radius \(r\). \[V(r_1)=V(r)\] The potential is therefore \[V(r)=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_1}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{D}\]
Key points
  • Electric field inside a perfect conductor is zero.
  • If \(\vec{E}=0\), then electric potential is constant.
  • The entire conducting shell remains at the same potential.
  • Potential due to charge \(q\) at radius \(r_1\) is \[V=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_1}.\]
Mistakes to avoid

  • Inside a conductor, potential is constant, not necessarily zero.
  • Do not use distance \(r\) if the shell potential is determined by radius \(r_1\).

questions.question: A steady current \(I\) flows through a long cylindrical wire of radius \(R\), find the magnetic vector potential at any point outside the conductor at radius \(r\). Vector potential on the surface of the conductor may be taken to be equal to zero.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] Magnetic vector potential due to a current element is \[\vec{A} = \int_{-L}^{L} \frac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi} \frac{I\,dx} {\sqrt{r^{2}+x^{2}}}\] From the figure, \[x=r\tan\theta\] \[dx=r\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta\] Substituting, \[\vec{A} = 2\int_{0}^{L} \frac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi} \frac{I\left(r\sec^{2}\theta\right)d\theta} {\sqrt{r^{2}+r^{2}\tan^{2}\theta}}\] Since, \[\sqrt{r^{2}+r^{2}\tan^{2}\theta} = r\sec\theta\] we get \[\vec{A} = 2\int_{0}^{L} \frac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi} I\sec\theta\,d\theta\] \[\vec{A} = 2\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi} \int_{0}^{L} \sec\theta\,d\theta\] Using \[\int \sec\theta\,d\theta = \ln\left(\sec\theta+\tan\theta\right)\] \[\vec{A} = 2\frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi} \left[ \ln\left(\sec\theta+\tan\theta\right) \right]_{0}^{L}\] Using \[\tan\theta=\frac{x}{r}, \qquad \sec\theta=\frac{\sqrt{r^{2}+x^{2}}}{r}\] \[\vec{A} = \frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi} \left[ \ln\left( \frac{\sqrt{r^{2}+x^{2}}}{r} + \frac{x}{r} \right) \right]_{0}^{L}\] \[\vec{A} = \frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi} \left[ \ln\left( \frac{\sqrt{L^{2}+r^{2}}}{r} + \frac{L}{r} \right) -\ln(1) \right]\] For \[L\gg r\] \[\sqrt{L^{2}+r^{2}} \approx L\] Hence, \[A = \frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi} \ln\left(\frac{2L}{r}\right)\] \[\boxed{ A=\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi} \ln\left(\frac{2L}{r}\right) }\]
Key points
  • Magnetic vector potential due to a current element is obtained from \[d\vec{A} = \frac{\mu_{0}I\,d\vec{l}} {4\pi R}.\]
  • Trigonometric substitution \[x=r\tan\theta\] simplifies the integral.
  • For a long conductor, \[L\gg r,\] the approximation \[\sqrt{L^{2}+r^{2}}\approx L\] is used.

questions.question: A monochromatic plane electromagnetic wave travels in vacuum in the positive X direction \((x,y,z\) system of coordinates). The electric and magnetic fields can be expressed as
questions.explanation:
For a uniform plane electromagnetic wave propagating in the positive \(x\)-direction, \[\vec{E}\times\vec{H} = \vec{S}\] where \(\vec{S}\) is the Poynting vector and indicates the direction of propagation. Given, \[\vec{E}(x,t) = E_0\cos(kx-\omega t)\,\hat{a}_y\] For propagation along \(+\hat{a}_x\), \[\hat{a}_y\times\hat{a}_z = \hat{a}_x\] Hence the magnetic field must be along the positive \(z\)-direction. Also, in a lossless medium (vacuum), electric and magnetic fields are in phase. Therefore, \[\vec{H}(x,t) = H_0\cos(kx-\omega t)\,\hat{a}_z\] Checking the options:
  • Option A: Correct direction and in phase.
  • Option B: Electric and magnetic fields are \(90^\circ\) out of phase, which is not possible for a uniform plane wave in vacuum.
  • Option C: Gives \[\hat{a}_y\times(-\hat{a}_z) = -\hat{a}_x\] which corresponds to propagation in the negative \(x\)-direction.
Hence, \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • Direction of propagation is given by the Poynting vector: \[\vec{S}=\vec{E}\times\vec{H}.\]
  • In vacuum, \(\vec{E}\) and \(\vec{H}\) are mutually perpendicular and are in phase.
  • For propagation along \(+\hat{a}_x\), \[\hat{a}_y\times\hat{a}_z=\hat{a}_x.\]
  • Magnitudes are related by \[E=\eta_0 H,\] where \(\eta_0\) is the intrinsic impedance of free space.

A \(240\,\text{V}\), dc shunt motor draws \(15\,\text{A}\) while supplying the rated load at a speed of \(80\,\text{rad/s}\). The armature resistance is \(0.5\,\Omega\) and the field winding resistance is \(80\,\Omega\).

A differentially compounded d.c. motor with interpoles and with brushes on the neutral axis is to be driven as a generator in the same direction with the same polarity of the terminal voltage. It will then
options: be a cumulatively compound generator but the interpole coil connections are to be reversed
be a cumulatively compounded generator without reversing the interpole coil connections.
be a differentially compounded generator without reversing the interpole coil connections
be a differentially compounded generator but the interpole coil connections are to be reversed.
questions.explanation: In a compound machine, both series and shunt windings are present. When the terminal voltage connection is reversed while running as a generator, the field pole polarity remains unchanged because the shunt field current direction remains the same. The direction of rotation also remains the same, hence the generated EMF retains the same polarity. Therefore, the armature current must reverse. Since interpoles are connected in series with the armature, their polarity automatically reverses with armature current. Hence, there is no need to interchange the interpole connections. In a differentially compounded machine, the shunt-field flux and series-field flux oppose each other. When the armature current reverses, the series-field flux reverses while the shunt-field flux remains unchanged. Thus, the two fluxes now act in the same direction and add together, causing the machine to behave as a cumulatively compounded machine without reversing the interpole connections. \[\boxed{B}\]

Out of the several characteristics shown in Figure, identify the appropriate ones to match the following. [figure unavailable]
(a)Speed--torque characteristics of induction machine under motoring operation.
[2mm] (b)Current--torque characteristics of a DC series motor.
[2mm] (c)Power factor variation with voltage of an induction motor under no-load operation.
[2mm] (d)Speed--torque characteristics of induction machine under DC injection dynamic braking operation.
[2mm] (e)Speed--torque characteristics of DC series motor.
questions.explanation:
The correct matching is \[(a)\rightarrow R,\qquad (b)\rightarrow U,\qquad (c)\rightarrow P,\qquad (d)\rightarrow S,\qquad (e)\rightarrow Q\] (a) Speed-torque characteristic of induction motor
The speed-torque characteristic of an induction motor is the inverse of the torque-speed characteristic. Hence, \[(a)\rightarrow R\] (b) DC series motor
In a DC series motor, at low values of armature current, the machine is unsaturated and flux is proportional to current. \[\phi \propto I_a\] Since \[T \propto \phi I_a\] we get \[T \propto I_a^2\] At high values of armature current, the machine saturates, so flux becomes almost constant. \[T \propto I_a\] Thus, curve \(U\) is the closest representation. Hence, \[(b)\rightarrow U\] (c) No-load induction motor
Under no-load, the current drawn by the motor is mainly magnetizing and core-loss current. With increase in voltage and constant frequency, flux increases linearly with voltage and hence magnetizing as well as core-loss current increases. Therefore, \[(c)\rightarrow P\] (d) DC braking of induction motor
When DC voltage is applied, the stator field is stationary and cuts the rotor conductors. This induces emf and produces braking torque. At zero relative speed, induced emf is zero and hence braking torque is zero. Therefore, \[(d)\rightarrow S\] (e) Speed variation of DC series motor
In a DC series motor, \[N \propto \frac{1}{\phi}\] At light load, current and flux are small, so speed becomes very high. At higher load, flux increases and speed decreases. Hence, \[(e)\rightarrow Q\] Therefore, the final answer is \[\boxed{B}\]

A three-phase, \(50\,\mathrm{Hz}\), \(415\,\mathrm{V}\), synchronous machine operates at rated voltage and at a leading power factor of \(0.9\). Shaft power is \(15\,\mathrm{kW}\) and the excitation emf is \(400\,\mathrm{V}\). If per phase resistance is \(0.5\) ohm, find the synchronous reactance. Neglect mechanical losses of the system.
questions.explanation:
Given parameters are \[V_L=415\,\text{V},\qquad E_L=400\,\text{V},\qquad P_{\text{sh}}=15\,\text{kW}, \qquad \cos\phi=0.9\;(\text{leading}),\qquad R_a=0.5\,\Omega.\] Calculation of the armature current \(I_a\):
The input power balance, accounting for the leading power factor and armature copper losses, is \[\sqrt{3}V_LI_a\cos\phi+3I_a^2R_a=P_{\text{sh}}\] Substituting the given values, \[(\sqrt{3}\times415\times I_a\times0.9)+(3I_a^2\times0.5)=15000\] \[646.92I_a+1.5I_a^2=15000\] Rearranging, \[1.5I_a^2+646.92I_a-15000=0\] Solving for the positive value of \(I_a\), \[I_a= \frac{-646.92+\sqrt{(646.92)^2-4(1.5)(-15000)}}{2(1.5)}\] \[I_a= \frac{-646.92+713.10}{3}=22.06\text{A}\] Phase-based vector analysis for \(X_s\):
Assuming a star-connected system, the per-phase terminal voltage is \[V_t=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}}\approx239.60\,\text{V}\] The per-phase induced EMF is \[E_f=\frac{400}{\sqrt{3}}\approx230.94\,\text{V}\] For a power factor of \(0.9\) leading, \[\sin\phi=\sqrt{1-(0.9)^2}\approx0.4359\] For a leading power factor alternator, \[E_f^2= (V_t\cos\phi+I_aR_a)^2+ (V_t\sin\phi-I_aX_s)^2\] Substituting the values, \[(230.94)^2 = (239.60\times0.9+22.06\times0.5)^2 + (239.60\times0.4359-22.06X_s)^2\] \[53333.28 = (215.64+11.03)^2 + (104.44-22.06X_s)^2\] \[53333.28 = (226.67)^2+(104.44-22.06X_s)^2\] \[53333.28 = 51379.29+(104.44-22.06X_s)^2\] Therefore, \[(104.44-22.06X_s)^2=1953.99\] Taking the positive square root for the standard inductive solution, \[104.44-22.06X_s=\sqrt{1953.99}\approx44.20\] \[22.06X_s=60.24\] \[X_s=\frac{60.24}{22.06}\] \[\boxed{2.73}\]
Key points
  • For a star-connected alternator, the phase voltage is \(V_t=V_L/\sqrt{3}\).
  • The input power includes both useful shaft power and armature copper losses: \[P_{\text{in}}=P_{\text{sh}}+3I_a^2R_a.\]
  • For a leading power factor alternator, the phasor relation is \[E_f^2=(V_t\cos\phi+I_aR_a)^2+(V_t\sin\phi-I_aX_s)^2.\]
  • The synchronous reactance obtained is the per-phase value.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use the line voltage directly in the per-phase phasor equation for a star-connected alternator.
  • Do not omit the armature copper loss \(3I_a^2R_a\) from the input power balance.
  • For a leading power factor, use the appropriate sign of the \(I_aX_s\) term.
  • In the quadratic formula, the discriminant contains \((646.92)^2\), not \((646.92)^3\).
  • Select the physically meaningful positive value of \(X_s\).

questions.question:
Two identical three-phase transmission lines are connected in parallel to supply a total load of 100 MW at 132 kV and 0.8 p.f lagging at the receiving end. The ABCD constants of each transmission line are \(A=D=0.98\angle1^\circ, B=100\angle75^\circ\ \Omega/\text{phase}, C=0.0005\angle90^\circ\ \text{S}/\text{phase}\) Determine:
  1. (a) The ABCD constants of the combined network.
  2. (b) The sending-end power factor.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Two identical transmission lines are connected in parallel. The ABCD constants of each line are \[A=D=0.98\angle1^\circ\] \[B=100\angle75^\circ\ \Omega\] \[C=0.0005\angle90^\circ\ \text{S}\] Since the lines are identical, \[A_1=A_2=A\] \[B_1=B_2=B\] \[C_1=C_2=C\] \[D_1=D_2=D\] (a) ABCD Constants of the Parallel Combination
For two identical networks connected in parallel, \[A_{eq} = \frac{A_1B_2+A_2B_1} {B_1+B_2}\] Substituting \[A_{eq} = \frac{AB+AB}{B+B}\] \[A_{eq}=A\] Therefore \[A_{eq} = 0.98\angle1^\circ\] Similarly, \[B_{eq} = \frac{B_1B_2} {B_1+B_2}\] \[= \frac{B^2}{2B}\] \[= \frac{B}{2}\] Hence \[B_{eq} = 50\angle75^\circ\ \Omega\] For \(C_{eq}\), \[C_{eq} = C_1+C_2+ \frac{(A_1-A_2)(D_2-D_1)} {B_1+B_2}\] Since \[A_1=A_2\] and \[D_1=D_2\] the additional term becomes zero. Thus \[C_{eq} = C+C = 2C\] \[= 0.001\angle90^\circ\ \text{S}\] Similarly, \[D_{eq}=D\] Hence \[\boxed{ A_{eq}=D_{eq}=0.98\angle1^\circ }\] \[\boxed{ B_{eq}=50\angle75^\circ\ \Omega }\] \[\boxed{ C_{eq}=0.001\angle90^\circ\ \text{S} }\] (b) Sending-End Power Factor
Receiving-end power: \[P_R=100\ \text{MW}\] Receiving-end voltage: \[V_R=132\ \text{kV}\] Receiving-end power factor: \[\cos\phi_R=0.8\] Therefore \[\phi_R = 36.86^\circ\] The receiving-end line current is \[I_R = \frac{P_R} {\sqrt3V_R\cos\phi_R}\] \[= \frac{100\times10^6} {0.8\times\sqrt3\times132\times10^3}\] \[= 546.73\ \text{A}\] Hence \[I_R = 546.73\angle-36.86^\circ\] The receiving-end phase voltage is \[V_R = \frac{132}{\sqrt3} \angle0^\circ\] \[= 76.21\angle0^\circ\ \text{kV}\] Using the transmission-line equation \[V_S=A_{eq}V_R+B_{eq}I_R\] \[V_S = (0.98\angle1^\circ) \left( \frac{132}{\sqrt3} \angle0^\circ \right) + (50\angle75^\circ) \left( \frac{546.73}{1000} \angle-36.86^\circ \right)\] \[V_S = 74.686\angle1^\circ + 27.33\angle38.14^\circ\] \[V_S = 97.87\angle10.706^\circ\ \text{kV}\] Similarly, \[I_S = C_{eq}V_R+D_{eq}I_R.\] Substituting, \[I_S = (0.001\angle90^\circ) \left( \frac{132}{\sqrt3} \angle0^\circ \right) + (0.98\angle1^\circ) (546.73\angle-36.86^\circ).\] Evaluating the individual terms, \[C_{eq}V_R = 76.21\angle90^\circ = j76.21,\] \[D_{eq}I_R = 535.80\angle-35.86^\circ = 434.65-j313.24.\] Hence, \[\begin{aligned} I_S &= (434.65-j313.24) +j76.21\\ &= 434.65-j237.03. \end{aligned}\] Therefore, \[I_S = 495.01\angle-28.70^\circ~\text{A}.\] The sending-end power-factor angle is \[\phi_S = \angle V_S-\angle I_S = 10.705^\circ-(-28.70^\circ) = 39.41^\circ.\] Hence, \[\text{Sending-end p.f.} = \cos39.41^\circ = 0.773.\] Since the sending-end current lags the sending-end voltage, \[\boxed{ 0.773\ \text{lagging} }\]

questions.question: In a string of three identical suspension insulator units supporting a transmission line conductor, if the self capacitance of each unit is denoted as \(C\) Farads, the capacitance of each connector pin to ground can be taken as \(0.1C\) Farads. Determine the voltage distribution across the string if the maximum permissible voltage per unit is 20 kV. Also determine the string efficiency.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Consider a three-unit suspension insulator string. Let the voltages across the top, middle and bottom (conductor-end) units be \[V_1,\qquad V_2,\qquad V_3,\] respectively. The self-capacitance of each unit is \[C,\] and the shunt capacitance from each metal fitting to the tower is \[kC,\] where \[k=0.1.\] Applying KCL at the junctions of the string, At the first junction,
the current through the top unit equals the sum of the current through the second unit and the shunt current. Hence, \[j\omega CV_1 = j\omega CV_2 + j\omega(0.1C)V_1.\] Dividing throughout by \(j\omega C\), \[V_1 = V_2+0.1V_1,\] or \[0.9V_1 = V_2. \tag{1}\] At the second junction,
the node voltage with respect to the tower is \[V_1+V_2.\] Therefore, \[j\omega CV_2 = j\omega CV_3 + j\omega(0.1C)(V_1+V_2).\] Dividing by \(j\omega C\), \[V_2 = V_3+0.1(V_1+V_2).\] Substituting (1), \[0.9V_1 = V_3+0.1V_1+0.09V_1,\] \[0.71V_1 = V_3.\] Hence, \[V_1 = \frac{V_3}{0.71} = 0.76336\,V_3,\] and from (1), \[V_2 = 0.9V_1 = 0.83969\,V_3.\] Thus, the voltage distribution is \[V_1:V_2:V_3 = 0.763:0.840:1.\] Since the conductor-end unit has the maximum permissible voltage, \[V_3=20~\text{kV}.\] Therefore, \[V_1 = 0.76336(20) = 15.27~\text{kV},\] \[V_2 = 0.83969(20) = 16.79~\text{kV},\] \[V_3 = 20~\text{kV}.\] Hence, the total string voltage is \[V_s = 15.27+16.79+20 = 52.06~\text{kV}.\] The string efficiency is \[\eta = \frac{\text{Total string voltage}} {n\times\text{Maximum unit voltage}} \times100,\] where \[n=3.\] Therefore, \[\eta = \frac{52.06}{3\times20}\times100 = 86.76\%.\] Hence, \[\boxed{ \begin{aligned} V_1 &= 15.27~\text{kV},\\ V_2 &= 16.79~\text{kV},\\ V_3 &= 20.00~\text{kV},\\ \eta &= 86.76\%. \end{aligned} }\]

questions.question: A three-phase delta-wye connected 30 MVA, 33 kV/11 kV transformer is protected by a simple differential relaying scheme. The CT ratio on the primary side is 500:5 and that on the secondary side is 2000:5. Sketch the CT connection diagram for the relaying scheme. Also calculate the relay current setting for faults drawing up to 200% of the rated current.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
The transformer is connected \[\Delta/Y\] and therefore introduces a phase displacement between the primary and secondary line currents. To compensate for this phase shift in differential protection:
  • CTs on the delta side are connected in star.
  • CTs on the star side are connected in delta.
This ensures that under normal operating conditions the currents entering the relay are balanced. --- The transformer rating is \[S=30\ \text{MVA}\] Primary voltage: \[V_1=33\ \text{kV}\] Hence rated primary line current is \[I_{L1} = \frac{30\times10^6} {\sqrt3\times33\times10^3}\] \[I_{L1} = 524.86\ \text{A}\] The relay is required to remain stable for faults drawing up to \[200\%\] of rated current. Therefore fault current considered for setting is \[I_f = 2\times524.86\] \[I_f = 1049.72\ \text{A}\] --- CT Secondary Current The CT ratio on the primary side is \[500:5\] Therefore secondary phase current of the CT is \[I_{CT} = 1049.72 \times \frac{5}{500}\] \[I_{CT} = 10.4972\ \text{A}\] Since the CTs on the delta side are connected in star, the relay sees the line current of the CT secondary circuit. Thus the relay current becomes \[I_r = \sqrt3\times10.4972\] \[I_r = 18.18\ \text{A}\] --- Relay Setting The relay has a standard 5 A current rating. Hence the relay setting is \[\text{Relay Setting} = \frac{18.18}{5}\] \[= 3.636\] Therefore, \[\boxed{3.636}\] or equivalently \[\boxed{363.6\%}\] relay setting.

The SCR is connected to an inductive load, where \(L=150\,\text{mH}\) in series with a small resistance and the supply voltage is \(200\,\text{V dc}\). The forward drops of all transistors/diodes and the gate-cathode junction during ON state are \(1.0\,\text{V}\). [figure unavailable]

Consider the thyristor circuit of figure. The thyristor is given a triggering pulse after every \(10\,\mathrm{ms}\). calculate the duration for which the thyristor remains ON after each triggering pulse. Assume ideal devices and explain briefly the basis. [figure unavailable]
questions.note: Answer: 0.733ms
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] When the thyristor turns OFF, \[i_{R}+i_{L}=0\] The resistor current is \[i_{R}=\frac{E}{100}\] The LC branch current is \[i_{L}=E\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}\sin\omega_{0}t\] where \[\omega_{0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}.\] Hence, \[\frac{E}{100} + E\sqrt{\frac{4\times10^{-6}}{10\times10^{-3}}} \sin\omega_{0}t =0\] Cancelling \(E\), \[0.01 + \sqrt{\frac{4\times10^{-6}}{10\times10^{-3}}} \sin\omega_{0}t =0\] Since \[\sqrt{\frac{4\times10^{-6}}{10\times10^{-3}}} =0.02,\] we get \[0.01+0.02\sin\omega_{0}t=0\] \[\sin\omega_{0}t=-\frac{1}{2}\] Taking the first valid solution, \[\omega_{0}t=\frac{7\pi}{6}\] Also, \[\omega_{0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\times10^{-6}\times10\times10^{-3}}} = 5000\ \text{rad/s}.\] Therefore, \[t_{\text{on}} = \frac{7\pi}{6\omega_{0}} = \frac{7\pi}{6\times5000} = 0.733\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}\] \[\boxed{0.733}\]
Key points
  • At turn-OFF, the resistor current and resonant LC current satisfy \(i_{R}+i_{L}=0\).
  • The natural resonant frequency is \(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}\).
  • The LC branch current amplitude is \(E\sqrt{C/L}\).
  • The first valid instant satisfying the current condition determines the thyristor turn-OFF time.

questions.question: Fringing in capacitive type transducer can be minimized by providing a
questions.note: Answer: Guard ring
questions.explanation:
In an ideal parallel plate capacitor, electric field lines are perfectly straight and confined between the plates. Ideally, \[E=\frac{V}{d},\qquad C=\frac{\varepsilon A}{d}\] These relations assume all electric field lines remain inside the plate area. \[\boxed{\text{Fringing Effect}}\] At the edges of capacitor plates, electric field lines spread outward instead of remaining straight. How guard ring helps A guard ring is a conducting ring placed around the sensing electrode and kept at the same potential as the main electrode. With guard ring, field lines terminate on the guard ring instead of spreading into space. [figure unavailable] Therefore answer is: \[\boxed{\text{Fringing Effect}}\]
Key points
  • Simple intuition: Guard ring “captures” stray field lines before they spread outward, so the capacitor behaves more like an ideal parallel plate capacitor.
  • Due to fringing:
    • effective plate area increases,
    • capacitance changes slightly,
    • measurement becomes inaccurate.
